patterns.label: I want to…
patterns.note: The most useful starter — attach any verb to express what you want to do.

drills.english: I want to watch a movie.

patterns.label: I'll have / I need…
patterns.note: Use for ordering food, asking for things, or stating what you need.

patterns.label: Do you have…?
patterns.note: A very natural way to ask about availability — literally 'have or not have?'

patterns.label: Where is…?
patterns.note: Put the thing you're looking for at the start, then ask where it is.

examples.j: sai2 sau2 gaan1 hai2 bin1 dou6?
dei6 tit3 zaam6 hai2 bin1 dou6?

patterns.label: How much?
patterns.note: Works alone or after pointing at something. Add ni1 go3 (this one) for clarity.

patterns.label: Please give me…
patterns.note: Very common in restaurants and shops. Note how 'me' comes at the end.

examples.j: m4 goi1 bei2 bui1 caa4 ngo5
examples.e: Please give me a cup of tea

examples.j: m4 goi1 bei2 go3 doi2 ngo5
m4 goi1 bei2 faai3 zi2 ngo5

patterns.label: Very…
patterns.note: hou2 intensifies any adjective. Stack it for extra emphasis — hou2 hou2 means 'very very good'.

patterns.label: Not / Don't…
patterns.note: m4 is the general negation particle. Place it directly before the verb or adjective.

patterns.label: Yes/no question
patterns.note: Add maa3 to the end of any statement to turn it into a yes/no question.

examples.j: nei5 sik1 gong2 gwong2 dung1 waa6 maa3?

patterns.label: What would you like to…?
patterns.note: A polite way to ask what someone wants — common in service situations.

examples.e: What would you like to eat?
What would you like to drink?
What would you like to buy?

patterns.label: I feel…
patterns.note: Use this to describe how you're feeling physically or emotionally.

examples.j: ngo5 gok3 dak1 m4 syu1 fuk6

patterns.label: Going to…
patterns.note: Simple and direct. Works for saying where you're going or asking where to go.

patterns.label: See you at / on…
patterns.note: Put any time word before gin3 to arrange when to meet.

patterns.label: Is that ok / Can I?
patterns.note: Literally 'ok or not ok?' — use to seek permission or check if something works.

examples.j: ngo5 co5 hai2 ni1 dou6 dak1 m4 dak1?
ji4 gaa1 heoi3 dak1 m4 dak1?

patterns.label: Too…!
patterns.note: Express that something is excessive. laa3 adds a sense of finality or mild complaint.

patterns.label: Can I / May I…?
patterns.note: A polite way to ask permission — more formal than dak1 m4 dak1.

examples.j: ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 gong2 maan6 di1?
ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 tai2 haa5?
ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 dang2 ngo5?

patterns.label: What is…?
patterns.note: Use when you want to know what something is called or what something means.

examples.j: ni1 go3 zi6 hai6 mat1 je5?

patterns.label: Why…?
patterns.note: Place dim2 gaai3 at the start of any statement to turn it into a 'why' question.

patterns.label: There's also… / And also…
patterns.note: Use to add something on top of what's already been said — great for ordering.

patterns.label: A bit more / less…
patterns.note: Adding di1 after an adjective softens it — useful for polite requests.

patterns.label: I like…
patterns.note: Express preferences for things, food, activities or people.

patterns.label: Give [someone] [something]
patterns.note: bei2 means 'give' or 'let'. The person receiving comes at the end — opposite to English.

patterns.label: I will…
patterns.note: Use wui5 to talk about future intentions or promises.

patterns.label: Have never / Not yet done
patterns.note: mei6...gwo expresses something you haven't experienced yet. Very useful for travel.

patterns.label: Already done…
patterns.note: zo2 marks completion — something has already happened. laa3 adds a sense of 'just now'.

patterns.label: How long?
patterns.note: Use to ask about duration — how long something takes or lasts.

examples.e: How long do I have to wait?
How long does it take to get there?

patterns.label: Together / Let's…
patterns.note: jat1 cai4 means 'together' — add it before any verb to suggest doing something jointly.

examples.e: Come on, let's do it together

patterns.label: First… then…
patterns.note: sin1 means 'first' and zoi3 means 'then/again' — use them to sequence actions.

patterns.label: I think…
patterns.note: ngo5 lam2 softly expresses an opinion or guess — less certain than stating a fact.

patterns.label: Wait a moment / Wait for…
patterns.note: dang2 means 'wait'. Use alone for 'wait a moment' or add who/how long to wait.

patterns.label: Greet, then speak
patterns.note: Cantonese conversations open with a greeting before getting to the point. Lead with a greeting, then say what you came to say.

examples.j: zou2 san4! sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6?
examples.e: Good morning! Have you eaten yet?

examples.j: nei5 hou2! hou2 noi6 mou5 gin3.

patterns.label: Match the time of day
patterns.note: Cantonese greetings change with the time of day — 早晨 in the morning, 晚上好 in the evening. Pick the one that fits.

examples.j: zou2 san4! fan3 dak1 hou2 maa3?
examples.e: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

examples.j: maan5 soeng6 hou2! sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6?
zou2 san4! gam1 jat6 faan1 gung1 aa3?

drills.english: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

patterns.label: Apologise
patterns.note: 對唔住 means 'sorry'. Lead with it, then explain — just like in English.

examples.j: deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 ci4 dou3.
deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 m4 zi1.
deoi3 m4 zyu6, m4 goi1 ze3 gwo3.
examples.e: Sorry — excuse me, let me through.

patterns.label: Respond to thanks
patterns.note: When someone says 多謝, the natural reply is 唔緊要 — 'it's nothing / you're welcome'.

examples.j: m4 gan2 jiu3, siu2 si6 laa1.
m4 gan2 jiu3, m4 sai2 haak3 hei3.
examples.e: You're welcome, no need to be formal.

patterns.label: Close a conversation
patterns.note: 再見 ends a conversation. It often follows a thank-you — 多謝，再見!

patterns.label: Answer yes or no
patterns.note: Cantonese has no single word for 'yes'. Reply with 係 (it is) or 唔係 (it isn't) to a 係-question.

drills.frameJ: keoi5 hai6 m4 hai6 hok6 saang1? — ▢.

patterns.label: Say if it's OK
patterns.note: 得 means 'OK / can do', 唔得 means 'no / can't'. A single word answers a 得唔得 question.

drills.frameJ: ji4 gaa1 heoi3 dak1 m4 dak1? — ▢.

patterns.label: Get attention politely
patterns.note: 唔該 is the everyday 'excuse me / please' — use it to get attention or ask for service. (多謝 is for thanking someone for a gift.)

patterns.label: Welcome someone
patterns.note: 歡迎 means 'welcome'. Shops greet customers with the set phrase 歡迎光臨 — 'welcome to our shop'.

patterns.label: Invite politely
patterns.note: 請 is the formal 'please', placed before a verb — 請坐 (please sit), 請講 (please speak). More formal than 唔該.

patterns.label: Counting up
patterns.note: Cantonese counts the same way you'd recite numbers in English: 一二三四五. The first ten numbers are the foundation for every larger number.

patterns.label: How many? (幾多)
patterns.note: 幾多 (gei2 do1) is the all-purpose 'how many / how much' question word. Use it before a classifier or noun to ask about quantity.

examples.j: nei5 jau5 gei2 do1 bun2 syu1?
examples.e: How many books do you have?

drills.english: How many books do you have?

patterns.label: Saying a dollar amount
patterns.note: 蚊 (man1) is the colloquial word for Hong Kong dollars. Just put a number in front: 十蚊 (ten dollars), 一百蚊 (a hundred dollars).

patterns.label: Half (一半)
patterns.note: 一半 means 'half'. Use it before a measure word + noun to say half of something — 一半個西瓜 = half a watermelon.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 sik6 zo2 ▢ go3 sai1 gwaa1.
drills.english: I ate half of the watermelon.

patterns.label: Multiples of ten
patterns.note: For 20, 30, 50 — just put the digit in front of 十: 二十 (twenty), 三十 (thirty), 五十 (fifty). Same pattern as English 'twen-ty', 'thir-ty'.

patterns.label: Asking someone's name
patterns.note: The standard opener for meeting someone new — 'What's your name?' literally 'you called what name?'

examples.j: cing2 man6 nei5 giu3 mat1 meng2?

drills.english: What is your name? — My name is William.

patterns.label: Introducing yourself
patterns.note: 我叫… is the natural way to introduce yourself — literally 'I'm called…'. Just add your name.

examples.j: nei5 hou2, ngo5 giu3 siu2 ming4.

drills.frameJ: A: nei5 giu3 mat1 meng2? B: ▢ William.
drills.english: What's your name? — My name is William.

patterns.label: How are you?
patterns.note: The standard 'How are you?' greeting after the initial 你好. Add 嗎 to turn 'you good' into a yes/no question.

examples.j: nei5 hou2 maa3? — ngo5 hou2 hou2.

drills.frameJ: A: ▢ B: ngo5 hou2 hou2, do1 ze6!
drills.english: How are you? — I'm well, thanks!

patterns.label: When you don't understand
patterns.note: 我唔明 is a polite, useful phrase to flag that you didn't catch what was said. Often paired with 請講慢啲 — 'please speak slowly'.

examples.j: deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 m4 ming4.
ngo5 m4 ming4, cing2 gong2 maan6 di1.
examples.e: I don't understand, please speak slowly.

drills.english: I don't understand — please speak slowly.

patterns.label: Asking the price
patterns.note: 幾錢？ literally 'how much money?' — the universal way to ask the price of anything at a shop or restaurant.

patterns.label: Who? (邊個)
patterns.note: 邊個 means 'who / which one'. Place it where the unknown person goes in the sentence.

examples.j: bin1 go3 hai6 nei5 ge3 lou5 si1?

patterns.label: What? (乜嘢)
patterns.note: 乜嘢 means 'what'. In Cantonese it usually goes at the END of the question — not the beginning like English. 你食乜嘢? = 'You eat what?'

patterns.label: Where? (邊度)
patterns.note: 邊度 means 'where'. Like 乜嘢, it usually goes at the end of the question in Cantonese.

patterns.label: When? (幾時)
patterns.note: 幾時 means 'when'. Often appears at the start: 幾時去食飯? = 'When are we going to eat?'

examples.e: When are we going to eat?

drills.english: When are we going to eat?

patterns.label: Why? (點解)
patterns.note: 點解 means 'why' — literally 'how to explain'. Use it to ask the reason for something.

patterns.label: Introducing a family member
patterns.note: 呢個係我… is the everyday way to introduce someone — literally 'this one is my…'. Add the family word at the end.

examples.j: ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 baa4 baa1.
ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 maa4 maa1.
ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 sai3 lou2.

patterns.label: Talking about parents
patterns.note: To talk about your mum or dad, just say 我媽媽 / 我爸爸 — no possessive particle needed. The relationship is built in.

examples.j: ngo5 maa4 maa1 hou2 sek3 ngo5.
examples.e: My mother loves me very much.

examples.j: ngo5 maa4 maa1 zyu2 faan6 hou2 hou2 sik6.

drills.english: My mother loves me very much.

patterns.label: Talking about siblings
patterns.note: Cantonese distinguishes elder and younger siblings with separate words — 哥哥 (older brother), 弟弟 (younger brother), 姐姐 (older sister), 妹妹 (younger sister). No ambiguity, but you have to know which.

examples.j: ngo5 go4 go1 duk6 daai6 hok6.
examples.e: My older brother is in university.

examples.j: ngo5 mui4 mui2 hou2 ho2 oi3.
examples.e: My younger sister is very cute.

examples.j: ngo5 jau5 jat1 go3 ze4 ze1.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 ▢ bei2 ngo5 daai6 loeng5 seoi3.
drills.english: My older brother is two years older than me.
drills.frameE: My … is two years older than me.

patterns.label: Grandparents (paternal vs maternal)
patterns.structure: je4 je2 / maa4 maa2 / ngoi6 gung1 / ngoi6 po4
patterns.note: Cantonese has different words for paternal and maternal grandparents. 爺爺 / 嫲嫲 are your father's parents; 外公 / 外婆 (with 外 meaning 'outside') are your mother's. The distinction matters in conversation.

examples.j: ngo5 je4 je2 zyu6 hai2 hoeng1 haa5.
examples.e: My (paternal) grandfather lives in the village.

examples.j: ngo5 maa4 maa2 zyu2 faan6 hou2 hou2 sik6.
ngo5 ngoi6 po4 hou2 sek3 ngo5.
examples.e: My (maternal) grandmother loves me very much.

drills.english: My paternal grandfather lives in the village.

patterns.label: Talking about your children
patterns.note: To say how many children you have, use 我有 + [number] + 個 + 兒子 (son) / 女兒 (daughter). 個 is the all-purpose classifier for people.

examples.j: ngo5 jau5 jat1 go3 ji4 zi2.
ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 neoi5 ji4.
